title: The Second Play
passages:
The drum screamed. Not a metaphor — the Marrow's winch, a salvaged capstan bolted to the keel and fed by a hydrogen cell that whined like a dying mosquito, was hauling two hundred kilos of unconscious diver through a vertical shaft of gray water, and the bearings had not been greased since the last storm season. Each revolution bit into the hull's ribs. Sol had the shutter cracked, one eye on the gate's red light, the other on the line disappearing through the moon pool. Dey sat lashed to the mast step, his chest hitching with the wet rattle of lungs that had traded their last clean breath for a child's life, fingers white-knuckled on a coil he could no longer work. Salas stood amidships, motionless, the line's bitter end wrapped twice around his forearm, the coil at his feet like a sleeping snake. He had not spoken since he broke surface fourteen months after the world wrote him off. Bayo Adisa was at the drum, bandaged hands finding the rhythm, shoulders squared against the surge that slammed the hull every twelve seconds.

Wren knelt at the comms console, slate cradled in her lap, the barnacled recorder from Salas's harness clipped to the input jack. The first play — Mara's voice, cool and precise, directing a diver to the second seal beneath Mercy General's pharmacy — had driven them here. One play left on the slate.

"Nia," she said into the mic. "Nia, hear me. Talk to me." Static. The carrier wave held, but the return was dead air. At thirty meters the scrubber canister had given up, the CO2 scrubbing media exhausted, and from there the clock was not depth or line speed but the acid already eating her blood. Wren's thumb found the advance stud on the slate. She needed to know who had opened the trunk's inner seal before Nia reached it. The inner seal, Nia had reported, breached from the inside. Recent. That meant someone had been down there after Mara sealed it. Someone who knew the cache existed.

The recorder spun up. A click of old gears. Then static, thick and wet, like the sea pressing its mouth to the speaker.

A man's voice. Not Mara's.

It read like a cargo count. That was the first wrong thing — the man on the slate wasn't afraid, wasn't even fast. He spoke the way a diver speaks when he's rationing breath and refuses to spend a single word on panic.

"Mercy General, service level," the voice said. "Forty-two meters on the anchor line. There's a pocket here, air's holding. I've got hours. Longer, if I don't talk too much." A dry sound that might have been a laugh. "I'll talk too much."

Wren's thumb came off the advance stud. She knew that cadence. She'd rebuilt it a dozen times off other crews' slates — the flat, itemized calm of a man reading his own manifest while the water decides about him.

The static pressed in, thick and wet. Then he gave a date. Fourteen months gone.

"Deckhand logged aboard the Marrow as Adisa, Bayo," the voice said. "He's topside, on the drum. I can see the soles of his boots through the moon pool. Line's fouled on the second seal below the pharmacy. I asked him to re-rig it." A pause. The hiss filled it. "He said he would. He gave me his word."

Nobody on the Marrow moved. Up at the shutter Sol had gone still as a piling, one eye yet on the gate's red light, her jaw set hard enough to ache. Dey's head had come up off the mast step, the wet rattle in his chest gone quiet.

"Then he cut it," the voice said. Calm. Patient. "Clean. Above the knot, so it wouldn't snag going up. I watched the tail of it go through the moon pool. I'm in the pocket at forty-two meters, and I'm going to run out of hours in here." Another pause. "If anyone plays this back — the man who left me is Bayo Adisa. He'll tell you it was the surge. It wasn't the surge."

The recording clicked and wound down into hiss, and kept hissing, the barnacled speaker pushing dead sea-noise out into the cabin.

Wren had thumbed the stud to learn who opened the inner seal before Nia reached it. The slate had given her a different name instead, and above them the drum hauled on under its own power, load set, bearings biting the hull every turn — hauling up a girl who was spending the same kind of hours.

Then boots rang on the companionway.

Bayo climbed up into the light. Both hands were wrapped to the knuckle, the bandage gray and smeared with grease where he'd been feeding the line. He came up two rungs, saw every face in the cabin turned toward him and the slate hissing in Wren's lap, and stopped.

"Whose tape is that," he said. Still warm. Still smiling, the smile already reaching for whatever it needed to fix. "Sol. Sol, that's not —"

Wren's hand closed flat over the slate.
